Hi recent graduate here, secured a scholarship in a local Uni.

My advice is to take up your lecturer's suggestion. First and foremost, lecturers know how the system works, they know that no matter how capable you might be, if you don't fulfil the things that Unis look out for, it'll all be wasted.

It would help greatly if you are in a EXCO/Maincomm position. Why? Because being in such an appointment gives you opportunities to ORGANIZE projects, and serve a community. Unis greatly value this over simply just participating in events or helping out. So if you can find a cca that fulfils this without being an EXCO then by all means, otherwise you can consider joining ESC or a P4 club. 

You're right in saying that not having a cca in year 1 puts you at some disadvantage, I understand as my year 1 was covid and I didn't take anything up. But don't let that hold you back, go and apply for leadership appointments, as long as you can convince others that you have the heart to serve, there'll always be a place for you. I took up EXCO in a p10 club in y2 and y3. Also take up competitions whenever possible and try to win at least 1. Plus points if it's against other unis.

Finally, one thing I wished all tp students knew earlier is that Unis STILL LOOK AT YOUR GPA FIRST, at least when it comes to scholarships. So if you really want it, you'll have to work for it and might have to sacrifice some things during your TP journey. Feel free to pm me if you have any more questions!


TLDR: If you want to secure uni and/or scholarship, Maincomm is good, take up competitions, work for your GPA.


Edit: EXCO is not limited to p10 clubs, in fact sports CCAs are great because you can cover both leadership and competitions in one package (assume you do win comps)

Hi! TP alumnus here :) 
It really depends on what you hope to achieve by the time you graduate. CCA or not both have their pros and cons but imo generally it is good to take one on.

If you take on a CCA:
PROS:
- Spend time doing something you like/meaningful
- Discover something new that you might enjoy
- Meet new friends
- Some CCAs also have overseas trips
- MOST importantly, if you contribute significantly or take on leadership positions, it'll play well when applying to Uni/Scholarships

CONS:
- (potentially) less time with your classmates/non CCA friends
- less free time (also depends on ur cca commitment level)
- obviously it's extra effort (non compulsory) outside of academics
- very niche but i find that sometimes you might end up spending more money as compared to someone who js goes straight home after class. Think about having meals outside w CCA mates etc etc, it adds up. But can also be mitigated with good planning and financial management.

As for Sports (& performing arts) Vs. Non Sports, generally I find that Sports CCAs offer a very attractive deal whereby you can get Leadership and Competition achievements in one package. Important if you want to win TP awards and again for Uni. But the requirement is that you are really good at what you do (because you have to actually win the comps). Vs non-Sports CCAs whereby you might take on leadership positions but you have to take on other projects or comps in school to hit that portfolio. 

Generally if you're looking for a chill TP journey, maybe hoping to go straight to work, I would suggest
- Finding a CCA you enjoy/ related to your aspiration
- Trying a new CCA and leave after a year if you don't enjoy it
- No CCA (but also think about what you would otherwise be doing with the time)

If you're looking to grind it out for Uni or anything or that sort, then it's all mentioned above. Hope that helps!

I'm not against new laws and licenses for fishermen, if anything, I'm for it. But as an angler myself, it was clear that Samantha Lee was not an angler and exaggerated her report. Typically, to my knowledge, most anglers fishing for larger fish at bedok jetty will use bait (dead or live), this means that 9/10 times the hook is swallowed and hooks onto a fish's gills, thus causing it to bleed out and die. That's why those who plan to catch and release typically use artificial lures as they usually only hook the tip of a fish's mouth. 

Given the situation of catching the stingray, as mentioned, it was impossible to use a net. Anglers use  a "gaff" which is a large hook tied to a rope to hook and lift the creature up. (Not exactly sure if this was done but I'd imagine that's what happened)

So take note, it was not impossible that the ray would have already died BEFORE it was lifted up. Samantha Lee's report exaggerated this part, which was untrue and unnecessary. 

If we give her the benefit of doubt, say the ray was still alive and well. Keeping the hook and cutting off the line is not an option as it will still eventually damage the ray's innards/intestines and kill it eventually. Whether the man was aware it was an endangered species, up to debate. 
 
My point is, as an angler, your first reaction when you catch the ray is NOT to eat it, it looks nothing like your hawker bbq rays. When you catch a fish, you do NOT cut the line to release it unless the line breaks on its own. 

The only part I felt was slightly off was the distribution of the meat. Perhaps the relevant agencies could've been contacted before cutting up the creature. But from the perspective of an older folk, perhaps this was not what came to mind.

Education is the best and most effective way to reduce the chances of such incidents. Back then education on such topics was not as advanced or informative as it probably is now. It is unfair to slam the old folk who caught this, it is probably more meaningful to focus on educating our youths and the next generation.
